v: Know which letters French does not pronounce
Read your first words out loud

b.v: 1) French drops the ends of words
The single biggest thing about French spelling: the last consonant is usually silent. Learn this and half of French pronunciation falls into place.

v: petit = puh-TEE — the t is silent
grand = grahn — the d is silent
vous = voo — the s is silent
beaucoup = boh-KOO — the p is silent

b.v: The exception is worth memorising as a word: C-R-E-F. c, r, f and l are usually pronounced at the end. Think of the English word CaReFuL.

v: è and ê = eh, as in mère, fête
ç = s, never k — français is fron-SEH
à, ù = the accent changes the meaning, not the sound

b.v: When a vowel is followed by n or m, the n disappears and the vowel goes through the nose. There is no English equivalent, so listen rather than read.
eau is three letters and one sound: oh. French does this a lot — spelling and sound part ways early.

v: Read all ten out loud twice
Say petit, grand, vous, beaucoup — drop the last letter each time

day-2.t: Day 2 — Greetings and tu vs vous

v: Greet at any time of day
Know when to say tu and when to say vous
Bonjour = hello, good day — the safe one, all day until evening
Bonne nuit = good night — only when going to bed

b.v: There is no separate 'good afternoon'. Bonjour covers the whole day.
French has two words for 'you'. vous is formal, and also plural. tu is for friends, family, children and colleagues who have offered it. Using tu with a stranger is not friendly, it is rude.

v: Ça va bien, merci = I'm well, thank you

b.v: If in doubt, use vous. A French person will say 'on peut se tutoyer' when they want to switch to tu.

v: Bonne journée = have a good day
Bonne soirée = have a good evening
Merci beaucoup = thank you very much
Je suis désolé(e) = I am sorry
Ask how they are, formally and casually
Say your name, age and where you are from
Ask the same of someone else
il / elle est = he / she is
vous êtes = you are (formal or plural)
il / elle a = he / she has

b.v: French says your age with avoir, not être. J'ai trente ans — 'I have thirty years'. Saying je suis trente sounds very odd.

v: Je m'appelle Khalid = my name is Khalid — literally 'I call myself'
Je viens du Pakistan = I come from Pakistan
J'habite à Lahore = I live in Lahore
Je parle un peu français = I speak a little French
Comment vous appelez-vous ? = what is your name? (formal)
Comment tu t'appelles ? = what is your name? (casual)
D'où venez-vous ? = where are you from?
Enchanté = pleased to meet you (a man says this)
Enchantée = pleased to meet you (a woman says this)

b.v: Say the whole introduction with your own details:

v: Bonjour. Je m'appelle ___. Je viens du ___. J'habite à ___. Enchanté.

day-4.t: Day 4 — le, la and why it matters

v: Learn the endings that give it away

b.v: 1) Every noun is masculine or feminine
There is no neuter in French. A table is feminine, a book is masculine, and there is no logic to find — it has to be learned with the word.

v: l'eau = the water — le or la shortens to l' before a vowel
les livres = the books (plural, same for both)

b.v: Learn 'la table', never 'table' on its own. This is the single habit that separates people who get French gender right from people who guess forever.
Unlike English, the describing word usually comes after the thing. And it changes to match.

v: un grand livre = a big book
une grande maison = a big house
un petit chat = a small cat
une petite table = a small table
Write ten nouns you know with le or la
Say them as pairs, never alone

day-5.t: Day 5 — Numbers and the strange seventies

v: Say prices and your phone number

b.v: About 25 minutes. One part of this is genuinely odd.
From 17 the pattern turns regular: dix-sept is literally ten-seven.
French has no separate word for seventy, eighty or ninety. It does arithmetic instead.

v: 71 = soixante et onze — sixty and eleven
99 = quatre-vingt-dix-neuf — four twenties, ten and nine

b.v: Belgium and Switzerland use septante and nonante for 70 and 90, which is much easier. France does not.

v: Combien ça coûte ? = how much does that cost?
Ça fait douze euros cinquante = that comes to 12.50
C'est trop cher = it's too expensive
Say your phone number digit by digit

b.v: About 30 minutes. The most useful lesson here.
Drop the -er and add the ending. parler (to speak) becomes:
je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent all sound identical. The endings are for the eye, not the ear.
3) Three irregular ones you cannot avoid

v: aller = to go: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont
faire = to do: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font
venir = to come: je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent

b.v: French wraps the verb in ne ... pas.

v: Je parle → Je ne parle pas = I do not speak
Il travaille → Il ne travaille pas = he does not work
In speech ne is often dropped: je parle pas
Est-ce que in front: Est-ce que vous parlez français ?
Flip the words: Parlez-vous français ? (most formal)
Conjugate aimer and travailler in full
Ask the same question all three ways
Order in a café or restaurant
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît = I would like a coffee, please
La carte, s'il vous plaît = the menu, please
Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ? = what do you recommend?
L'addition, s'il vous plaît = the bill, please

b.v: Je voudrais is the polite way to ask for anything. Je veux means 'I want' and sounds like a demand.

v: Je ne mange pas de porc = I do not eat pork
Je suis végétarien(ne) = I am vegetarian
Sans alcool, s'il vous plaît = without alcohol, please
Est-ce qu'il y a du porc dedans ? = is there pork in it?
J'ai faim = I am hungry — literally 'I have hunger'

b.v: Order a coffee and a sandwich, ask what they recommend, ask for the bill — out loud, in one go.

v: Où est la gare ? = where is the station?
Où sont les toilettes ? = where are the toilets?
Comment aller au centre-ville ? = how do I get to the town centre?
tout droit = straight ahead — careful, not 'to the right'
la première rue à droite = the first street on the right

b.v: tout droit means straight on. à droite means right. They look alike and mean different things — this catches everyone once.

v: Un billet pour Paris, s'il vous plaît = one ticket to Paris, please
Aller simple ou aller-retour ? = single or return?
À quelle heure part le prochain train ? = when does the next train leave?
Buy a return ticket to Lyon
Give directions to your own house in French
lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche

b.v: Days and months are not capitalised in French. Writing Lundi looks wrong to a French reader.

v: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin
juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre
Quelle heure est-il ? = what time is it?
Il est trois heures = it is three o'clock
trois heures et quart = quarter past three
trois heures et demie = half past three
quatre heures moins le quart = quarter to four

b.v: French uses the 24-hour clock for anything official. A train at 19h30 is dix-neuf heures trente.

v: Quel temps fait-il ? = what is the weather like?
Il fait beau = the weather is nice
Il fait chaud = it is hot
Il fait froid = it is cold

b.v: Weather uses faire: il fait chaud is literally 'it makes hot'.
Read it out loud twice, then cover the English.

v: B: Bonjour. Comment vous appelez-vous ? — Hello. What is your name?
A: Je m'appelle Khalid. Je viens du Pakistan. — My name is Khalid. I come from Pakistan.
B: Enchanté. Vous parlez français ? — Pleased to meet you. Do you speak French?
A: Un peu. Excusez-moi, où est la gare ? — A little. Excuse me, where is the station?
B: Tout droit, puis à droite. — Straight ahead, then right.
A: Combien coûte un billet pour Paris ? — How much is a ticket to Paris?
A: Merci beaucoup ! Au revoir. — Thank you very much! Goodbye.
Read French out loud without guessing at silent letters
Greet formally and casually, and know which to use
Handle le and la, and know why it matters
Order food and buy a ticket
Tell the time and talk about the weather
The past tense: j'ai mangé, je suis allé
Object pronouns: le, la, lui, leur

b.v: French listening is harder than French reading, because words run together. Start with slow news for learners before jumping to films.
Record yourself reading the conversation above. Keep it. Do it again in a month.
